newsitem.title: UK: Inco strike boosts physical nickel, outlook cloudy.
newsitem.headline: Inco strike boosts physical nickel, outlook cloudy.

text.p: A strike at Inco Ltd's Sudbury operation has injected some life in Europe's physical nickel market, but traders are uncertain about the longer term picture.
"There has been some near-term scrambling to cover and quite a bit of interest for the medium term," one trader said.
Inco's 4,670 unionised workers at its Sudbury operation went on strike at midnight on Monday, June 2 and the Canadian firm said on Tuesday it was seeking the help of a provincial mediator.
The Ontario division is expected to produce 230 million lb of nickel this year, Inco said.
An extended strike could push nickel futures back up to their recent highs, traders and producer sources said.
"If you don't have a settlement by end-June, you'll see $8,000 again," one said.
Problems with gas supplies at Russia's Norilsk was also a potentially bullish element in the market.
LME three months nickel touched its year's peak of $8,325 per tonne on March 4, but prices have fallen back to end Wednesday's afternoon kerb at $7,260.
Stainless steel mills, which have been using high ratios of scrap, are taking advantage of the weak prices, one trader said.
"The market is picking up...the price is low and some are quite prepared to take standard metal," he said.
But a source at a producer of high quality nickel said they had not yet been approached by any mills.

Premiums for Western plating metal, cif Rotterdam, were slightly firmer at $290/$330 per tonne over LME cash, up from $280/300. But uncut Russian material has sunk to a deeper discount of $70/110 from $40/$80 last month.
The situation with scrap supply was unclear, with some saying there was abundant material arriving from Eastern sources and others warning that the situation was becoming tight.
Nickel-in-scrap as a ratio of LME cash had firmed over the past six months from 90 percent to 95 percent, indicating a market largely in balance, sources said.
Stainless steel mills have been using large quantities of scrap in their operations this year as they run at very high capacity.
There is concern, however, that not all of the output is being absorbed by end-users and may be going into producer stocks.
"One has to be wary about the fundamental demand side, the mills may have to cut output in the second half," a producer source said.
An early Inco settlement and weaker demand from the stainless sector could send prices to fresh lows, he added.
LME broker Brandeis this month cut its view of 1997 average three month nickel prices to $8,117 per tonne from $8,598.
Stainless steel inventories were still historically high and the second half may see production cuts, especially in Southeast Asia, it said in a report.
--Eric Onstad, London Newsroom +44 171 542-8065
